title: Subprime Lender Goeasy Sees Elevated Writeoffs Before Business Improves
content: Subprime lender Goeasy Ltd., which surprised investors weeks ago with a surge of bad debts in its vehicle financing business, said it expects loan writeoffs to remain elevated for a while before getting better later in the year.

title: Brazil’s Braskem Said to Plan Court Protection Against Creditors
content: Braskem SA, Brazil’s largest petrochemical company, is considering seeking protection in local courts against its creditors, according to people involved in the talks.

title: Why Carson Block Is Placing Bearish Bets on Credit ETFs
content: Carson Block, founder and CEO of Muddy Waters Research, explains his bearish outlook on credit markets, highlighting expectations for credit spreads to widen significantly. He speaks during an interview on "Bloomberg The Close." (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Carson Block Lays Out Bearish Credit ETF Bets Amid AI Fears
content: Famed short seller Carson Block is placing bearish bets on some of the biggest corporate credit ETFs as a way to hedge the risk of economic malaise caused by AI.

title: Lenders to Vista's Software Firm Solera Form Pact as Loans Near Maturity
content: A group of senior lenders to Solera Holdings Inc., including Apollo Global Management Inc. and Pacific Investment Management Co., has tapped a legal adviser ahead of the software company’s debt maturing in 2028, according to people familiar with the situation.

title: Carson Block Warns About AI, Talks ETFs and Credit Spreads
content: Muddy Waters Capital founder and CEO Carson Block says investors are underestimating the risk AI poses to the labor market and US economy. Speaking on "Bloomberg The Close," Block also comments on credit spreads and where he is finding investment opportunities. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Crypto Get Easier Path to 401(k)s
content: Bloomberg's Loukia Gyftopoulou, joins Scarlet Fu and Tim Stenovec on "Bloomberg Crypto." Companies offering alternative assets in retirement savings plans would get more legal protection under a new Trump administration proposal. The changes could make it easier for 401(k) plans to include private credit, private equity, crypto and real estate investments. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Petro’s ‘Worst Mistake’ Saves Colombia Central Bank From Turkey’s Fate

title: FW: 01/04/26: Die sechs Commerzbank-Szenarien, Comeback zweier Digitalbanker
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Wednesday, 1 April 2026 06:20:08 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 01/04/26: Die sechs Commerzbank-Szenarien, Comeback zweier Digitalbanker Außerdem: Deutsche Bank holt Fintech-Topshot, Mosen bleibt N26-Vorstand [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/0c399ede-6ac8-7960-0cc2-0578e6f0ef55.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=69600b5cda&e=8f69674dd2> Die Schlacht um die Commerzbank  diese sechs Szenarien sind jetzt noch denkbar Als die Italiener einstiegen, damals, im Jahr 2019, da taten sie das zunächst mit etwas unter 10%. Doch dann stockten sie sukzessive auf und hielten an ihrem Akquisitionsziel, einem bekannten deutschen Großkonzern, bald mehr als 25% der Anteile. Es entwickelte sich ein schleichender Übernahmekampf, zunächst noch ohne offizielles Angebot, aber geprägt von steigendem strategischem Druck, zumal die italienische Seite immer wieder auf die europäische Konsolidierungslogik verwies, der sich die Beteiligten letztlich nicht entziehen könnten. Dass es sich um eine politisch delikate Branche handelte? Dass das deutsche Zielobjekt über einen Ankerinvestor verfügte, der sich den Übernahmeplänen lange Zeit entgegenstellte? All das schien die Italiener nicht wirklich zu interessieren. Sie hatten hinreichend tiefe Taschen. Sie hatten erstaunlich viel Geduld. Und es ging ihnen erkennbar nicht um irgendwelche Sympathiepreise. Sondern: Sie wollten einfach nur diesen deutschen Konzern übernehmen. Wenn auch nicht um jeden Preis. Das erste Angebot, abgegeben im Mai 2025 und mit da noch knapp 30% Anteil, wurde noch sehr niedrig angesetzt. Erst mit dem verbesserten zweiten, im Juli 2025, erreichten sie schließlich ihr Ziel. Nach einer langen, aufreibenden Übernahmeschlacht gehört ProSiebenSat 1, also der drittgrößte deutsche Medienkonzern, jetzt zur Berlusconi-Holding MFE ("Mediaset"). Kurz gesagt: Braucht man sich angesichts der frappierenden Parallelen also gar keine Illusionen mehr zu machen, dass die Commerzbank eine Übernahme durch die Unicredit noch wird verhindern können? Ist das Playbook längst geschrieben und wird nun nur noch orchestriert? Ja, könnte so sein. Aber: Noch ist der Kampf um die Commerzbank nicht entschieden. Das Einzige, was wirklich feststehen dürfte: Von hier an gibt es eigentlich noch sechs denkbare Szenarien, wie die Sache jetzt ausgehen kann. Wir haben uns die Freiheit genommen, die sechs Szenarien einfach einmal fein säuberlich für Sie zu skizzieren  bitte sehr: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e4a9312632&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/d46bbd62-80d4-271d-88da-592379b8c188.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=bd538eced7&e=8f69674dd2> Agentic Commerce verschiebt die Kontrolle im digitalen Handel: KI-Agenten übernehmen Suche, Auswahl und zunehmend auch den Kauf selbst. Das verändert Marktstrukturen, Payments und Geschäftsmodelle grundlegend. Unser Whitepaper zeigt, wer künftig die entscheidenden Schnittstellen kontrolliert und wie sich Unternehmen jetzt strategisch positionieren sollten. Hier gehts zum Download<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=505da1dc32&e=8f69674dd2> Personalien Mosen bleibt N26-Vorstand  und weitere rund 60 Personalien aus dem März: Obwohl bei N26 dieser Tage ein neuer CEO aufschlägt (nämlich der bisherige UBS-Manager Mike Dargan), wird Interimschef Marcus Mosen dem Führungsgremium der Berliner Neobank auch weiterhin angehören  und zwar als einfacher Vorstand für Recht, Personal und Regulatory Operations, wie das Fintech am Dienstag dem "Handelsblatt" bestätigte. Ursprünglich war die Öffentlichkeit (und auch der ein oder andere Beteiligte) davon ausgegangen, dass sich Mosen im Zuge von Dargans Ankunft zurückziehen werde. Auf welchen Zeitraum das neue Mandat für den 61-Jährigen angelegt ist, blieb gestern unklar, ebenso, ob es sich um eine Vollzeitstelle handelt. Fest steht lediglich, dass das neue N26-Vorstandsteam damit nun komplett ist: Neben Dargan und Mosen gehören noch Risikochef Jochen Klöpper und Finanzchef Arnd Schwierholz dem Gremium an. Sämtliche Personalien aus dem März, darunter auch ein paar ganz frische (etwa: "Deutsche Bank holt Fintech-Topshot" und "Das Comeback zweier prominenter Digitalbanker") haben wir hier für Sie zusammengefasst: FS Premium (die Deutsche-Bank-Personalie ist frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=cea6e7e5ac&e=8f69674dd2> Blog Weniger Retail wagen  EZB legt bei neuer Payment-Strategie den Fokus auf B2B: Die EZB hat am Dienstagmorgen ihre neue (bzw. erstmals seit Jahren aktualisierte) Retail Payments Strategie vorgestellt. Die sichtbarste Neuerung: Die Retail Payments Strategie heißt gar nicht mehr Retail Payments Strategie". Sondern nur noch Payment Strategie. Das Retail ist raus, der reduzierte Name zugleich neues Programm. Hier die sechs wichtigsten Takes: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=3a1807d9e2&e=8f69674dd2> Ticker * Die DZ Bank fährt ihr Verbund-Exposure runter. April 2026 Der Tag Das Wichtigste aus der Wirtschaft ­ [https://cdn.prod.www.manager-magazin.de/images/b2d157b2-58c7-44d8-b7fa-ebafabb8933a_w112_r1_fpx48_fpy55.jpg] Christoph Rottwilm Redakteur manager magazin Lieber Herr Frignani. Seit Freitag vergangener Woche ist die Broker- und Investmentzunft in Deutschland geradezu euphorisiert: Der Bundestag hat nach dem Debakel mit der Riester-Rente eine Reform der Altersvorsorge beschlossen <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D> . Anlegerinnen und Anleger sollen hierzulande ab Januar 2027 Geld vom Staat dazu bekommen, wenn sie in ETFs, Fonds und ähnliche Vehikel investieren. Das private Altersvorsorgedepot sorgt auch bei den jungen Onlinebrokern für Goldgräberstimmung: Meine Kollegin Hannah Schwär, die sich in der Branche umgehört hat, berichtet von der Hoffnung auf Millionen neue Kunden und Milliarden an mobilisiertem Kapital (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>. Bis es so weit ist, müssen Anbieter wie Trade Republic oder Scalable Capital allerdings noch ihre Hausaufgaben machen: Noch gibt es keine passenden Produkte, und die Anpassung der Infrastruktur und Workflows an das neue Gesetz dürfte anstrengend werden. Viel Geld werden die Unternehmen mit dem staatlich geförderten Programm ohnehin kaum verdienen, denn die Gebühren sind gedeckelt. Die Euphorie bei den Finanzvertrieben bezieht sich daher auf eine andere Aussicht: Die Reform verspricht ihnen Millionen neuer Kunden, denen sie weitere, margenträchtige Produkte offerieren können. Folge: Der Dax legte am heutigen Mittwoch zeitweise 3 Prozent zu, die Ölpreise gaben deutlich nach<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>. * Die führenden Wirtschaftsinstitute zeigen sich weniger optimistisch: In ihrem Frühjahrsgutachten haben sie ihre Prognose für das Wachstum des Bruttoinlandsprodukts wegen des Irankriegs halbiert<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>. Auch 2027 könnten die Folgen des Kriegs die Wirtschaft weiter belasten, so die Ökonomen. * Seid verschlungen, Milliarden: OpenAI hat erneut eine gigantische Finanzierungsrunde abgeschlossen. Amazon<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D> , Nvidia, Softbank und andere steckten zusammen 122 Milliarden Dollar in das amerikanische KI-Start-up (ChatGPT)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>, dessen Börsengang noch in diesem Jahr erwartet wird. Damit beläuft sich der Wert von OpenAI inzwischen auf 852 Milliarden Dollar (zumindest auf dem Papier). [separator] Der Fauxpas des Tages: * Eine weitere News aus der Welt der künstlichen Intelligenz wirkt dagegen geradezu tröstlich menschlich: Die US-Firma Anthropic, ebenfalls einer der weltweiten KI-Vorreiter, hat bestätigt, dass sie versehentlich Teile des Quellcodes ihres Chatbots Claude veröffentlicht <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D> hat. Ein Anthropic-Sprecher begründete den bereits zweiten Fehler binnen einer Woche mit menschlichem Versagen. Technisches Versagen als Begründung wäre für das Unternehmen vermutlich auch deutlich unangenehmer gewesen. [separator] Kopf des Tages: [Rückkehr ins Finanzgewerbe: Jörg Kukies geht zu Morgan Stanley] Rückkehr ins Finanzgewerbe: Jörg Kukies geht zu Morgan Stanley Hannes P Albert / picture alliance / dpa * Einmal Banker, immer Banker: Jörg Kukies (58) war Co-Chef der deutschen Tochter von Goldman Sachs und damit einer der einflussreichsten Investmentbanker der Republik, bevor er 2018 als Staatssekretär ins Bundesfinanzministerium wechselte (unter dem damaligen Minister Olaf Scholz; 67). Später wurde der SPD-Mann Kukies kurzzeitig selbst Bundesfinanzminister, doch nun folgt die Rückkehr in sein angestammtes Gewerbe: Wie meine Kollegin Katharina Slodczyk erfahren hat, geht Kukies demnächst zur US-Bank Morgan Stanley, wo er eine Toprolle übernehmen wird (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>. [separator] Meine Empfehlung für den Abend: [Skyline von Doha, Katar: Arabische Staatsfonds könnten der Welt den Geldhahn abdrehen] Skyline von Doha, Katar: Arabische Staatsfonds könnten der Welt den Geldhahn abdrehen Juergen Tap / Hoch Zwei / IMAGO * Der Irankrieg erschüttert den arabischen Raum und sendet Druckwellen in die Weltwirtschaft. Offenkundig ist die Störung der weltweiten Öl- und Gasversorgung. Weniger sichtbar dagegen: Auch der Kapitalfluss, der sich aus der Region am Golf auf die Finanz- und Kapitalmärkte rund um den Globus ergießt, könnte versiegen. Die Staatsfonds von Katar, Saudi-Arabien, Abu Dhabi und anderen Ländern der Gegend gehören seit Jahren zu den wichtigsten Investoren der Weltbörsen. Was passiert, wenn diese Fonds verstärkt versuchen sollten, daheim die Folgen des Kriegs zu lindern? Dieser Frage ist mein Kollege Lukas Heiny nachgegangen  hier finden Sie die Antworten (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>. The traditional simple arithmetic is that a lot of people want to buy shares of a big company, but when the company is private, not that many people can. When the company goes public, many more people can buy its stock, so it should be worth more: All the retail investors and public-market funds and non-ARK ETFs will finally be able to buy it, and they will, so its stock will go up. One model of shareholder activism is that shareholders control the company, they elect the directors, and if they dont like what the directors are doing they can vote them out. In practice this is pretty hard: To vote out the directors, an activist shareholder has to launch a proxy fight and convince a majority of shareholders to vote for her slate, and the board has tools to delay or impede this. But at least in theory, and sometimes in practice, shareholders really can vote out the board and install new management, and this possibility gives them leverage. And so the directors and executives are responsive to shareholder demands, because they operate in the shadow of binding shareholder votes<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/h6wKOvk4IfVggVrMmQdRpyowBas7SK_AG9mCKLu0udopqYmuaMQX-k7HIjGVWuoEMwH9ONrvSuVwykoeWiKKYtnheGosr7Y7vU942FybRjL8ThOmjx3gQROec0nEwByrow5gYccMNB4Cr_Xqf7uHXGNppTctx27CnHAWpgIoCiTDa_pTgr0YAcfZlrui9EQm8bA8p3A_VyKFGlvusB77YHLVScijoVAavwn9eSqdlqj2Mj2ku1Fzjz67v1ykVwo_VvE_ZLK938dHi_SPLWIUIhrgzdVX9Zru4LlBWU164RKPVCIOKVIUtuEDFrxCZHEXIeX7jHnenZ8XFShAVFBL_b6MI-3OwHtUtrT-SYbQHG3sGxaX96W-vx6uxLQ/EU0oYQHODmhS5Xp7UoJ4tyniEhyMRN0q/19>. Another model of shareholder activism is that directors and executives are responsive to shareholder demands not because of the threat of a proxy fight but because, come on, we are all professionals here and we all want the same thing. It is good for everyone  the executives, the directors, the activist shareholders  if the stock goes up. The executives and directors have fiduciary duties to the company; they are supposed to make the stock go up. They are chosen for their skills and experience and energy, and they are compensated with stock and options to give them the right incentives. If an activist shows up, the board will thoughtfully engage with her, take her ideas seriously, and either implement them or provide some rational explanation, grounded in shareholder value, for why not. And if the shareholder doesnt like the explanation, her main tool to push back is not a proxy fight but embarrassment. Directors want to do the right thing for shareholders, and they want to be seen to do the right thing for shareholders. Being a successful director  one who presides over a rising stock price and is beloved by shareholders  is good for your career; doing good work on a good board can get you more board seats and other business opportunities. Plus youre probably in a golf club with other public-company directors and executives, and you want to be respected at the golf club. If an activist is out publishing nasty letters about how youre destroying shareholder value, that is motivating on its own. The proxy fight  the theoretical possibility that you will actually be kicked out of your directorship  is a minor footnote. These theories have a great deal of overlap in most companies: If a board is doing the wrong thing for shareholders, that might both embarrass them at the country club and lead to a proxy fight. But there is an important area of non-overlap: Lots of companies have dual-class shares that concentrate voting power in the hands of controlling shareholders (generally founders, etc.), so that the public shareholders really cant vote out the board. If the managers and directors are doing a bad job, the shareholders have no formal power to change things. But they can still write letters. They can still try to persuade the board to make changes, and the board still has some fiduciary duty to listen, and if the board ignores the shareholders and the stock keeps sliding, that will be embarrassing at the club. This was arguably something new in corporate finance, a new sort of asset that a company could have. If a company became a meme stock, it could go sell a lot of stock at very high prices and use the proceeds to pay down debt or hire executives<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/jmWrz_1Lzv5M2WLVnq2wun-eRqWdjBtsIlzwxEJe-gUbJgEasyUZXhL-Ox7CzZG5GRo0xcRVy9a7uAWT420jFiZ1_3QvM-hpUVzt1-apItaII7dqU3e7Y0Rey71ScE1JcqUqlj-izQpipRxDLazZuo8AjdM5iOhzoTxhVyMIl2UG22LPTIkdaTSAH531NSm5FC6_SvRj07ewvuDwJzIE2-Rh5a-PSzKEE6voNjIG7koUaXKLUSbbc4qomuJpyG7qmN7CbEZ8XCwMWexpczRwjUcKSL3Ow7tK6nfDlOrKkJmmW-m71TZuwQDNGAzV0fd1gziDnxmc8XtpTXnMnKjAhO_X9_iUaPZm17WQy5yhadLMoMVwaHgWwL-lFQk/bJGL5dqpS3n2CsCJwLOfG4NJgR16n1uD/19> or do acquisitions. If you are a creative financial engineer, though, you might not stop there. Thats just the low-hanging fruit. The deep analysis is that the discovery of meme stocks gave every smallish US public company a valuable new asset. Every company has some probability of becoming a meme stock: Theres always a chance that some small random company will catch fire with online retail investors and its stock will zoom up. And so the trick, if you are are a small public company that is not currently a meme stock, is converting that probability into cash now. You have some asset  your chance of becoming a meme stock  that has a real but uncertain value. Surely some hedge fund would pay you something for it. But how do you structure that deal, and what is the going rate for it? Theres actually a longstanding, though somewhat disreputable, financial instrument that fits the bill. Its what you might call a floating-strike convertible. Schematically the trade is: 1. A hedge fund gives a company $100 now. 2. In return, the company promises to give the hedge fund $100 worth of stock, whenever the hedge fund asks for it over the next few months or years. (And the hedge fund can split it up: Get $10 today, $20 in a week, $30 more in a month, etc.) 3. But $100 worth of stock is calculated in a weird way. For instance, it might be calculated as $100 divided by the lowest daily stock price over the last 10 trading days. [1] So if the companys stock trades at about $2 per share for a week, and then the next week it becomes a meme stock and trades at $5, $10, $15, $69 and $420, then the hedge fund will exercise its option and say okay Id like $100 worth of stock, at $2 per share thats 50 shares. And then it will sell those 50 shares for $420 each, or $21,000 total. Usually there are other bells and whistles, but here I want to focus on that lookback. Because it can convert its $100 into stock at the lowest price over some previous period, the hedge fund has a valuable option. In particular that option pays off if the stock goes up a lot, even briefly. [2] The hedge fund hands over its $100, it waits to see if theres a meme moment, and if there is it cashes out. If there is not a meme moment, the hedge fund just converts its $100 into stock at the market prices and sells it down over time. This tends to have the effect of depressing the stock price: The hedge fund gets some stock at $2 per share, it sells that stock, the stock goes down to $1.50, the hedge fund gets more stock at $1.50, it sells that, the stock goes down to $1, the hedge fund gets more at $1, etc. These deals are sometimes rudely called death spiral convertibles<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/JgoVrrxVn_ECsybRhNPG62xNTB3X7XgP3SV_VpkFlKlaZWBWUlyLbN-Jbo_RhY_N86H3hWaUd_vTIpgnBLU_Dp6z2dAaddcHIp1enciFt_Io4o9qKK9A76Nx26E9e0Vu2SHWds474PSVFIRPO0OFeYorTVcn1MJjbkEmcHfbuL8uyzaAxCchesS8wZVu8SEEn_c62b_sDw9loGCs7k7_wZip0rjRm_bI1KB9q82lgVncsr1zj2y5UPOKDBeCmilE0QUX-bK5iSS6jCcanh1YuTj1mCfWhBO1UYz0VGcwwhbEhGaqJR-1Fy-czXuxosW-cztdnO2uAH_MWtfOw_PDOKxx292SdAjwivlho6CsMRFMx3y-YXOWqb532kU/s23BgVfOuNPID6XzjOUrIkJruELWrI8E/19>. The bad outcome is a death spiral. In the olden days, you could have a computer scan a document  say, an earnings-call transcript  and try to pick out good words (profit) and bad words (loss). If there were a lot of good words, the news was good and youd buy the stock; if there were a lot of bad words, youd sell. This might work at some rough statistical level, and if you have no better ideas you could give it a try, but it is obviously pretty crude. Sometimes profit will be in a sentence like we had no profit, and is actually bad. A human, reading the transcript, would be able to pick up on subtleties of sentiment that are not reflected in mere counts of bad words. Modern machine learning tools are much better at holistically analyzing a document and telling you if the sentiment is good or bad. Pop the transcript into ChatGPT, ask it how do the executives feel, and it will give you a nuanced answer. Or you can probably automate that and quickly get a pretty precise sentiment score that can inform your trading decisions. Still, at least some crude rules of thumb work pretty well. If you count 73 swear words in an earnings-call transcript, something has probably gone wrong. You dont need to read the rest to get a nuanced understanding of sentiment. title: FW: 02/04/26: Bafin rügt Sparkassen-Tochter, Was sich bei der MaRisk ändert
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Thursday, 2 April 2026 06:19:59 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 02/04/26: Bafin rügt Sparkassen-Tochter, Was sich bei der MaRisk ändert Außerdem: Payment-Snippets, Fintech-Persos, Schwache Baufi-Zahlen [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/2b64dace-540a-2c1f-2e94-1fab164d8558.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=db273b9b20&e=8f69674dd2> Wochen-Podcast (KW 13&14) Die Deutsche Bank hat jetzt eine offizielle "Nummer 2"  und eine inoffizielle [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/08896b25-c6b3-2b3c-37b5-f92ec49d7919.jpg] Die Themen diesmal: #1: Die Zinsen steigen, aber die Einlagenkunden merken's nicht  wie unsere Banken gerade wieder an der Marge schrauben #2: Die Deutsche Bank hält an der Girocard fest. Weil der Kunde das so will, oder weil es politisch nicht anders geht? #3: Wholesale vs. Retail CBDC  was hinterm Shift in der Payment-Strategie der EZB steckt #4: Der Streit um das Altersvorsorge-Depot  verzerrt der Staat den Wettbewerb oder belebt er ihn womöglich sogar? #5: Revolut hat letztes Jahr in Deutschland rund 800.000 neue Kunden gewonnen. Was sind das für Kunden? #6: Bei allem Hype um Revolut  wenn man die Konto-Angebote nebeneinander legt, ist N26 auch nicht schlechter #7: Manche Banken haben gar keine Lösung für die CEO-Nachfolge  die Deutsche Bank hat jetzt gleich zwei Auf geht's: Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c940e9ebf2&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/5a5fb09d-4b52-a86b-1d14-63a3a50e632d.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=79af33c1e9&e=8f69674dd2> Klarheit in der Geldwäscheprävention: Mit der EU-AML-Verordnung steigen die Anforderungen an Daten, Prozesse, Governance und Dokumentationen erheblich. Für Finanzdienstleister ist jetzt der richtige Zeitpunkt, den eigenen Status zu überprüfen. Der AML-VO Quick-Check von Sopra Steria liefert in wenigen Minuten eine kompakte Standortbestimmung. Jetzt den Quick-Check durchführen!<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=85a10e18b6&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Morgan Stanleys fetter Coup  Jörg Kukies wird Deutschland-Chef des US-Instituts: Ist ja nicht so, als wäre Jörg Kukies nicht auch für andere Positionen gehandelt worden. Er könnte neuer Bahn-Chef werden, lautete im Sommer ein (freilich wildes) Gerücht. Er könnte Christine Lagarde als Präsidentin der Europäischen Zentralbank ablösen, spekulierte im Herbst die "Süddeutsche Zeitung". Doch stattdessen  kehrt der frühere Goldman-Sachs-Manager, langjährige Staatssekretär und kurzzeitige Bundesfinanzminister nun also zurück ins Investmentbanking. Allerdings nicht zu Goldman Sachs. Sondern (wie gestern Früh als erstes die Kollegen vom "Manager Magazin"/Paywall<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=dbbd77bee3&e=8f69674dd2> berichteten) zu Morgan Stanley, also dem ewigen Goldman-Rivalen ... ... Entsprechend der in seinem Fall offenbar abgestuften Karenzfristen wird Kukies ab Mai zunächst für sechs Monate zu Morgan Stanley nach London gehen. Erst danach soll er die eigentlich für ihn vorgesehene Position als Länderchef für Deutschland und Österreich übernehmen; parallel werde er auch den Vorsitz der in Frankfurt ansässigen EU-Einheit übernehmen, also der Morgan Stanley Europe SE. Aus Sicht des US-Instituts (das hierzulande ja immer ein bisschen im Schatten von Goldman Sachs oder J.P. Morgan Chase steht) ist die Verpflichtung ein veritabler Coup; Kukies wiederum darf sich darauf freuen, künftig wieder wie ein Investmentbanker zu verdienen (und nicht wie ein Politiker); und in gewisser Weise ist die Personalie auch eine Auszeichnung für die Bankenbranche als solche. Denn um wie ein Banker zu verdienen, muss man heutzutage ja nicht mehr zwingend einer sein. Blog Exklusiv: Deutliche Mängel  Sparkassen-Tochter "S-Rating" gerät ins Visier der Bafin. Die Risikodienstleister der Verbünde (bei der ParcIT war es ja ähnlich, siehe hier,<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=b972eede96&e=8f69674dd2> hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=4bc23e5d3c&e=8f69674dd2> und hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=1218db1f98&e=8f69674dd2>) haben offenbar erhebliche Probleme mit der Umsetzung neuer regulatorischer Vorgaben. Kommen auf die Institute vor Ort nun höhere Kosten zu? Unsere exklusive Recherche: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=778640bdf8&e=8f69674dd2> Die geplante Neufassung der MaRisk  hier kommen die wichtigsten Änderungen: Die Bafin hat wie angekündigt eine deutlich entschlackte Neufassung der MaRisk zur Konsultation gestellt  mit Lockerungen vor allem für "kleine" (<5 Mrd. Euro Bilanz) und "sehr kleine" Institute (<1 Mrd. Euro Bilanz). Also vor allem für viele Sparkassen und Volksbanken. title: Apollo’s Zelter Calls Private Credit Concerns Growing Pains
content: Apollo Global Management Inc. President Jim Zelter launched a full throated defense of private credit, downplaying investor concerns and describing recent developments in the asset class as mere “growing pains.”

title: Blue Owl Limits Redemptions on Private Credit Funds After Massive Exit Requests
content: Blue Owl Capital Inc. will limit redemptions from two of its private credit funds after facing a surge in withdrawal requests that is unprecedented among major firms in the $1.8 trillion market.

title: Dealmaking Competition Erodes Junk Loans’ Last Line of Defense
content: Relaxing covenant requirements to win competitors in the race to fund deals is leaving sub-investment grade loan investors without their last line of defense, according to an analysis by Moody’s Ratings.

title: Apollo’s Zelter Says Private Credit Concerns Are Just Growing Pains
content: Jim Zelter, president at Apollo Global Management, offers a defense of private credit and says investors are missing the plot on the public/private convergence. (Source: Bloomberg)

Binary bonds Yessss heres a trade: 1. You give me $100. 2. I spend $96.90 buying a US Treasury bill that will mature at $100 in February 2027. 3. I spend $2 buying Kalshi event-market contracts (that is, sports bets) on the Los Angeles Rams winning the pro football championship<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/vqkF7buEX7kz6sUPXnS2HN04XnNqQFqYIMP0EL-DG43jdYR36w8y4hpW-a2oVQBYFaX7ksqwppKjjETQAw8YpINIA-GQSQvbJrWAZkGkAUbXY5JuCaLeetm_Cv-F3Aop3r7WvQKvt72gHcvTvV43sIRyn8PPbqQBXChpks7r9x5-t8RvBewndL82r_1WVJc1MDHTIwtGDv4niXrXQFokUSXQZgpTM8I1nkLF_b0VBhzgyyAjuRGnZ8r5AjMesbg4WXl3fsWUokWcmKjrZjlus8aNk7aXRnVYrlZevVJVSy2k5yO2AcChYZZ1GSGs2x1w6KX1o_RwYlhkK1TdKB1use2zPSDuCn0BpN7et3Lz4dUNHywQzZiA04WmLQ/Zxqq4le1NfedOKVDbJrJNaafdeRgHUcr/19> in February 2027. (The pro football championship is the Super Bowl<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/iyKtlS_IwEdqIAeHSlBR12KEPv9m0e_Wdh9OMlE-18B_At3VB_8_AHB-7luzUzrTKE66gkqQ6zu30_QpdLfaKAihk5kCp-qWC88RC1JNtl5Qfrf2noDBaXiGRLnXeY_kzRBX6s_JCp_k_O7bOBq-mBE7ji30wQCXSkcR9dqMI16LZYFsxbyfGrNtiNZmWmFO73GxSFfiDiU-DeMHMTP3OU_5DDFyF1q2FWu6tzG5Y_IckQTO9X_Hv4jo7a1jR-Q4UxC0FUm7q3edhLHpH68ZWYdtubLlvfdRTh7h-SSujlufZRCdrxAsgzWsYmEi8HKteOn7uaCW2vk43msjnCmnRso7oWm8BqkItSt-bjHDM3TX9_8n9Ni1aU1QhQ/37XNV5OcC0bYPBkqgoSt2jodWSkoPAmG/19>.) The Rams have the best odds on Polymarket right now, but there are 31 other teams, and the Rams probability of winning is only 10%. I can buy 20 contracts for my $2. If the Rams win the Super Bowl, those contracts will pay out $20; if not, they will pay out $0. 4. I keep the other $1.10 for myself; Ive earned it. 5. In February 2027, I will pay you back $120 if the Rams win the Super Bowl, or $100 if they dont: I will hand you the payoff of the Treasury bill plus the payoff of the Kalshi contracts. What is this trade, from your perspective? Well, I mean, its sort of like you have bought a bond from me, and the bond pays interest, and you have wagered all of your interest on the outcome of the Super Bowl. Its a bond plus a football bet. But of course the financial industry is full of trades with the form a bond plus an unrelated derivatives bet. They are traditionally called structured notes, or structured products. They are sold, often by financial advisers, as a single package, a bond issued by a bank or broker with a payoff that varies based on some index or fact. The point is that the derivatives bet is fully embedded in the bond. The structured note is not a bond plus a separate derivatives bet; the derivatives bet is in the bond. This product thus has the following potentially interesting features: 1. Your financial adviser could sell it to you. (As opposed to your bookie.) I have a cool new structured product, she tells you. It offers 100% principal protection and high potential upside. The upside is risky but uncorrelated. 2. Shes right: Your returns on this trade depend on the Rams winning the Super Bowl, which is probably uncorrelated to the rest of your investment portfolio. (It might be correlated to the rest of your sports gambling portfolio!) Investors love<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/ai7Ce-APHfOjV099NDjtd9tPXozboxPyvbNqIgrKUU-Ve3DGLP7qEaVfyQYPyKGEMWEZfq-n9i0B0bX-2LPOG22gvKSPOgt5CptbfEBoPoEcv2A5UkUEcGYnZ93cL4j7m5SPakuPODmijknEuVUmtbVjBi5tGca5A54i5rFIRFX0CWZzTuJAeXqkMLmzHNGJCHF-ofogno8iIFMmbUItDqNbtbDS_U6MuFIOdM_Q5DXqDuJl3Fd29lBvFUXLe-75rkfUepY87gkKl3Q9je06goAmQFbI7BAgKKZyJ4YzqUGZdeuiC9sIzyvekyoWZpV6D2X1fRFX8btkctB8j-py8McBBTod3OTdRfZD6c9vo_FnuX60VlA5BXu_AA/82OjjFPtEFFmC_dph7PZoCIsaKOeGFsj/19> uncorrelated returns. 3. If you are a Rams fan, you might find this structured note more appealing than some other structured note with a higher expected value but no embedded football bet. 4. If you are a Seahawks fan, you might find this structured note appealing as a hedge against the risk that the Rams win the Super Bowl. (Or you might want a similar note that pays 20% if the Seahawks win.) 5. If your spouse, or your accountant, or your boss at the mutual fund where you work, asks you about this note, you can be like oh yes, thats a structured note that I purchased from a reputable broker-dealer. It has a lot of embedded optionality. Uncorrelated returns! Convexity! To your spouse or accountant, this looks like a securities trade, because it is a securities trade. You have bought a bond. It sits in a securities custody account at your broker, it has a CUSIP, its cash flows work like all of your other bonds. The issuance is the latest sign of how Wall Street firms are trying to harness the fast-evolving energy of prediction markets, which have so far attracted interest primarily from small retail traders. Marex was able to create the note because prediction markets like Kalshi offer it a place to hedge its risks as the odds move over time. As a non-bank structured notes provider, Marex doesnt take market risk with its issuance and fully hedges itself using derivatives. Marex is going to effectively build our own prediction market structured products, and then leverage Kalshi and other exchanges to replicate that, said Nilesh Jethwa, chief executive of Marex Solutions, a unit of Marex. The downside of strict liquidity terms, for a hedge fund manager, is that when your performance is bad your investors complain to the press about your liquidity terms. The upside is that they cant take their money out. The correct sequence, for a money manager, is roughly: 1. Have good performance. 2. Now everyone wants to get into your fund. 3. Let them in, but demand a long strict lockup: The only way they can get access to your hot in-demand fund is by agreeing not to take their money out for a long time. 4. Raise as much money as you can on those strict terms. 5. Now you can have bad performance! Obviously Step 5 is not necessary and is, in fact, bad; better to keep having good performance. The point is that, if you execute Steps 1 through 4 correctly, Step 5 is an option. If you dont, it isnt. Your job is to keep managing money. Having good performance is a necessary element of that job, but it is not a permanently necessary element. Really you can replace performance there with, like, marketing, or really anything that makes people want to get into your fund. The core sequence is: People want to get into your fund, you demand a lockup to let them in, and then later, when they want to get out, you say no. Companies, employers or retailers that want to sell customers prescription drugs can use CareValidates technology and network of online doctors to set up a business. The companys software connects patients with doctors and pharmacies, which write, fulfill and ship the prescriptions. CareValidate charges fees for its software. Mr. Gallagher saw an opportunity for his own telehealth business. CareValidate has the doctors and pharmacists and ships the drugs, which it gets from other companies that have factories. Presumably some humans work at the factories, and the doctors and pharmacists are also humans. Have US ground troops entered Iran? Last weekend, Bloomberg Weekend had a great story by Christopher Beam<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/VH0lC-PBhFEULa9KilFPfimFiuCtgBrLRISqFL3ump9CiSm8UUnrov9IzXb8QLJUDTZyaDF29iOwcRYguLMLbBcfsaM512vygHL9W9Tm9b2SEeiT569AwI76YjBXaRSpQjVG0OmXATNEqPCcZknH6rJfM5rt8HnF_PHAKf1yfVQZjjs0gMG54XM5xhzr_Nf-7434HqlU4K3txy7rVlTbpMLJ7uC6TzpZbR4hJfDHOh9JtldIDixBlfS_hfv4Od9FY7wxecHAkOSQ8gEQuaWpKwfqxMWfJDgPLJs6u0EXi1tv-xMre-a7uknBwQr9Ol5cNHy16-ozVPZfMPP4RwZhFdNqFNLSZhE0KlSES1wBeFu3msVuJd8RZjyieA/NalegO7u38rNOveCmv4V0J_SxZWex2N0/19> about how linguists are annoyed at Kalshi. Kalshi is a prediction market where you can bet on sports and various other events, including mentions markets, where a contract pays $1 if Jerome Powell says a certain word at a press conference or whatever, and $0 if he doesnt. But what are the boundaries of a word? Are singular and plural nouns the same word? Past and present tense verbs? Participles? Etc., all these boring disputes. Kalshi has some rules to resolve these questions, and linguists have criticisms: Karlos Arregi, a linguistics professor at the University of Chicago, says they appear to be arbitrary rather than based on a particular theory or philosophy of language. This looks like the kind of rules youd have in a game like Scrabble, he says. Its obvious to me these rules were not done by a linguist. Rivka Levitan, a professor of computer science and linguistics at Brooklyn College CUNY, describes them as more legalistic than linguistic. A good set of rules, she suggests, ought to prioritize logical consistency. Instead, Kalshis rules seem to draw lines for no clear reason. They allow for certain types of inflections (such as -s for plural) but not others (such as -ed, -ing, -er, or -est). If the strike word  that is, the one listed on the mention market  is veteran, then veterans counts. But if the strike word is veterans, then veteran doesnt count. This is unambiguous, but its also illogical. Similarly random-seeming are rules that allow deviations from the strike word when it comes to meaning but not form: If traders bet on a football announcer mentioning wind, for instance, their bet still hits for the clock winds down. But if the strike word is run, then ran or running doesnt count. Arguably what Kalshi needs is not a team of linguists but a team of philosophers: It offers a huge variety of contracts that pay off if some event occurs, but the boundaries of event and occur are not always crisp. Beam notes: it also reflects the broader challenge prediction market platforms face in their attempt to reduce reality to a series of yes-or-no bets. ... Many of the best-known disputes involve angels-on-a-pinhead-type debates: Did Cardi B perform at the Super Bowl? Did Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wear a suit? Did the US invade Venezuela? I suppose this is not unique to prediction markets. More legalistic than linguistic is a decent description of a lot of payoff disputes we have discussed around here. Is that US forces entering Iran? The Polymarket contract rules say: This market will resolve to Yes if active US military personnel physically enter Iran at any point by the listed date (ET). Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No". Military special operation forces will qualify; however, intelligence operatives will not count. .. US military personnel must physically enter the terrestrial territory of Iran to qualify. Entering Irans maritime or aerial territory will not count. The resolution source will be a consensus of credible reporting. Note: Only US military personnel who deliberately enter the terrestrial territory of Iran for operational purposes (e.g., military, humanitarian, etc.) will qualify. Pilots who are shot down, or other cases in which US military personnel do not deliberately enter the terrestrial territory of Iran, will not qualify. My reading of (1) those rules and (2) the credible reporting that I have seen suggests that the answer is yes: The officer who was shot down doesnt count, but at least some of the hundreds of special operations troops presumably deliberately enter[ed] the terrestrial territory of Iran to rescue him. (Definitely a lot of folks sitting around on Easter Sunday waiting to find out if a rescue helicopter touched down or just dropped some rope, a reader emailed me.) The April 30 contract is priced at close to 100%, suggesting that the market agrees that this counts; a Yes resolution has been proposed but as of this morning is still disputed. Various commenters on Polymarket complain: A pilot rescue should be considered as an intelligence operative and not a military landing. And: The market rules are unambiguous: only deliberate physical entry of US military personnel into Irans terrestrial territory qualifies. Aerial presence, downed pilots, or rescue scenarios explicitly do NOT count. And, most angels-on-a-pin-ishly: The verb enter denotes a single act, namely the moment of crossing into Iran. In this scenario, that crossing occurs while personnel are inside a helicopter, i.e., within Irans aerial territory. The rules explicitly provide that Entering Irans maritime or aerial territory will not count. Therefore, the only identifiable act of entry is expressly excluded by the rule. Once inside Iran, any subsequent landing or disembarkation does not constitute a new act of entry, but merely continued presence within the territory. I disagree, but I also sympathize; the headline US forces enter Iran by ... does suggest a terrestrial invasion, not a search-and-rescue operation, however large and coincidentally ground-based. These rules were not written by a philosopher of war. [2] Does this matter? I mean, no. Prediction markets are derivatives markets, where people compete to outsmart each other in zero-sum games. Being smart about technicalities and rule interpretation is a good and standard and normal way to make money in derivatives markets, as we talk about all the time. If prediction markets allow more people to be fleeced by reading the rules wrong, or to fleece others by reading the rules right, then hey great whatever. content: Goldman Sachs Group says its private credit fund narrowly escaped a broader exodus due to its reliance on institutional investors. Goldman Sachs Private Credit, which manages a so-called non-traded business development company, met redemption requests in the first quarter amounting to 4.999% of its outstanding shares. content: Get a jump start on the US trading day with Matt Miller and Dani Burger on "Bloomberg Open Interest." Deal or destruction. Markets on edge as war tensions collide with tech’s surprising resilience, even as a hidden helium shortage could disrupt AI and chip production. Bill Ackman makes a bold play for the world’s biggest music label. And Fed official John Williams says inflation risks may rise, but policy is holding steady. Not everything is securities fraud A thing that sometimes happens is: 1. Two companies agree to a merger. The buyer will buy the target at some premium to its current stock price. 2. They put out a nice press release saying things like we are doing this merger and here is the price and we expect it to close in the third quarter. 3. The targets stock price goes up to reflect the premium in the deal. 4. The next step is getting antitrust approval. 5. The deal does not get antitrust approval. Antitrust regulators decide that it is bad for competition, so they block it. 6. The targets stock price goes down. title: Private Credit Worries Result of 'Imbalances,' PIMCO's Karoui
content: PIMCO's Multi-Asset Credit Strategist Lotfi Karoui said concerns building in direct building are a little related to rapid growth. The ongoing exodus from nontraded vehicles, which make up 60% of the sector’s assets, and elevated leverage in their publicly-traded counterparts are key drivers of the credit grader’s revision, according to a report Tuesday. The “disruptive force” presented by artificial intelligence is expected to compound the group’s worries and put it “on defense” in the coming year, Moody’s analysts wrote. An abrupt reversal in the first quarter spurred the first ever net outflow for the sector, Moody’s said. Before artificial intelligence advances set off alarm bells over the durability of software securities, the vehicles had experienced robust net inflows as recently as the third quarter of 2025. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Private Credit Experiencing 'Growing Pains,' SLR Capital Partners' Co-CEO Gross
content: Michael Gross, Co-Founder of SLR Capital Partners said pressure on business development companies are part of private credit's "growing pains." JPMorgan Chase & Co. is restricting some lending to private credit funds after marking down the value loans in their portfolios. At the same time, BDCs — which lend directly to middle-market companies — are seeing elevated redemption requests amid fear of loss related to oversized exposure to software firms disrupted by AI. Besides equity from limited partners and public investors, private credit funds rely on banks for funds. They also raise debt in the investment-grade bond market. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: FW: 08/04/26: Akzeptanz-Pflicht für Kartenzahlungen? Die Coba im Orcel-Style
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Wednesday, 8 April 2026 06:15:27 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 08/04/26: Akzeptanz-Pflicht für Kartenzahlungen? Die Coba im Orcel-Style Außerdem: Wero-Rückschlag, Iwoca nennt Umsatzzahlen, Schufa siegt [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/3d823b6e-4d8c-9105-b09b-c5c3ff98551c.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0745c104c3&e=8f69674dd2> Commerzbank und Unicredit: Sie haben gesprochen!!! Und jetzt??? Huch, was war das denn? Und was sollte das? Also, falls es irgendwer von Ihnen nicht mitbekommen haben sollte, liebe Leserinnen und Leser: Unter dem herrlich nichtssagenden Titel "Commerzbank bekräftigt Potenzial der bestehenden Geschäftsstrategie" hat ebendiese Commerzbank gestern Mittag (es war zugegebenermaßen schon 14 Uhr, also nicht ganz Highnoon) eine Mitteilung verschickt, in der einfach mal ein bisschen aus dem Nähkästchen geplaudert wurde. Orcel-Style, sozusagen. Wenngleich beim Aufsetzen des Statements eine Goldwaage behilflich gewesen sein muss. Auf diese haben all die IR'ler, Juristen und Spin-Doktoren nämlich jedes Wort einzeln gelegt, bevor sie es dann mit samtbehandschuhten Fingern in die Tastatur eintippten. Die erste Quintessenz der Mitteilung: Die Commerzbank und die Unicredit haben endlich, endlich, endlich miteinander gesprochen! Auch wenn in der Mitteilung genau genommen nicht von Gesprächen die Rede ist. Sondern von Interaktionen: * "In den vergangenen Wochen fanden mehrere Interaktionen statt [...], um Grundlagen und Potenziale des von der Unicredit [...] in Aussicht gestellten Angebots zu einer Übernahme [...] konstruktiv zu eruieren." Die zweite Quintessenz: Gebracht hat's nix! * "[Die] Interaktionen haben [...] aus Sicht der Commerzbank kein ausreichendes Wertschöpfungspotenzial für ihre Aktionäre über die jetzige Standalone-Strategie hinaus aufgezeigt." Und was heißt das nun und wie geht's weiter? Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ce8096ddc5&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/af3711a9-5e8a-1b41-1e2d-752222593696.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=4e413181c4&e=8f69674dd2> Agentic Commerce verschiebt die Kontrolle im digitalen Handel: KI-Agenten übernehmen Suche, Auswahl und zunehmend auch den Kauf selbst. Das verändert Marktstrukturen, Payments und Geschäftsmodelle grundlegend. Unser Whitepaper zeigt, wer künftig die entscheidenden Schnittstellen kontrolliert und wie sich Unternehmen jetzt strategisch positionieren sollten. Hier gehts zum Download<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=24a6987839&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Exklusiv: Abgang von IBB-Vorständin Kemmner  was in den ersten März-Tagen wirklich passiert ist. Es wirkte alles reichlich sonderbar  auch wenn es das angeblich gar nicht war. Bereits in der ersten Märzwoche berichteten Quellen gegenüber Finanz-Szene, dass sich das Internationale Bankhaus Bodensee und seine langjährige Vorständin Heike Kemmner eher abrupt getrennt hätten. Nachdem das Institut unsere entsprechenden Nachfragen tagelang ignorierte, verschwand am Morgen des 9. März (das war der Montag der zweiten Märzwoche) schließlich Kemmners Name aus dem Impressum. Kurz darauf erreichte ausgesuchte Medien schließlich eine Pressemitteilung, wonach Kemmner "den Aufsichtsrat bereits im letzten Jahr darüber informiert" habe, "ihren laufenden Vertrag nicht zu verlängern". Zum 8. März (also an dem Sonntag) sei die Managerin nun "in enger Abstimmung mit dem Aufsichtsrat" aus dem Vorstand ausgeschieden. Also alles ganz normal? Ein Abgang, von langer Hand geplant? Wer's glaubt ... Bitte sehr: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=aadc6e837a&e=8f69674dd2> News * Das britische Kredit-Fintech Iwoca nennt erstmals Ertragszahlen für den deutschen Markt. Im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr hätten sich die hierzulande erwirtschafteten Umsatzerlöse auf 41 Mio. Euro summiert, sagte Deutschland-Chef Fabian Platzen dem "Handelsblatt"  verglichen mit dem Vorjahr eine Steigerung um rund 40%. Seit mittlerweile zwei Jahren arbeite man dabei profitabel. Wie Iwoca überdies bekannt gab, haben die eigenen Investoren die Refinanzierungslinie für den deutschen Markt um weitere 125 Mio. Euro auf nunmehr 350 Mio. Euro aufgestockt. * Der jahrelange Rechtsstreit um die Speicherdauer von Negativmerkmalen bei der Schufa und anderen Auskunfteien ist beendet. Nachdem eine bislang anhängige Klage vor dem OLG Köln zurückgezogen wurde (dorthin hatte der BGH den Fall zuletzt zurückverwiesen), gilt nun das erstinstanzliche Urteil des Landgerichts Bonn aus 2024. Dieses besagte, dass die Schufa negative Merkmale wie eine nicht beglichene Kreditrate bis zu drei Jahre speichern darf  selbst wenn der Vorfall zwischenzeitlich geheilt wurde (also der Kredit abbezahlt wurde). Kurz Bei den Verantwortungsträgern der Volksbank Brawo, gegen die die Staatsanwaltschaft Braunschweig wegen möglicher Untreue ermittelt (siehe unseren Genobanken-Ticker von letzter Woche<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=61d0dd58f3&e=8f69674dd2>), handelt es sich laut "Handelsblatt" um Vorstandschef Jürgen Brinkmann und ein weiteres Vorstandsmitglied. Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/9223036f-733c-e8dd-c231-189a0c69960a.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=f6be403830&e=8f69674dd2> Jetzt neu bei Finanz-Szene  unser Direktbanken-Letter: Wie antworten DKB und ING auf den Angriff von Revolut? Egan-Jones CLO* Summary Report
April 2026      *All Egan-Jones ratings in this report are non-NRSRO ratings
Still soft issuance levels – at a time when credit yields are reaching recent lows, CLO issuance continues to be weak, perhaps reflecting concerns regarding credit quality. CLOs issued in March decreased from 106 ($48.2B) in 2025 to merely 67 ($27.6B) in 2026<https://egan-jones.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81&id=b13cba0ff9&e=a1880c1820>. Note, these levels were a drastic drop from the Nov. 2024 highs of 127 deals and $54.6B. The 5-year treasuries are moderately low at 397 bps<https://egan-jones.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81&id=b1d633668d&e=a1880c1820> while the ICE US High Yield OAS is also near an annual low at 317bps, well below the high of 461bps in April 2025<https://egan-jones.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81&id=970d987f46&e=a1880c1820>. Regarding CLO credit quality, WARS has improved slightly (see chart below left). The CCC+ or lower rated CLO assets have been stable to slightly down recently as indicated in chart I-D. Regarding asset and tranche coupons, as can be seen in the chart below right both have dipped. Attached is a sample CLO report.
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/06f71d93-8c49-9d80-b1af-1a307e02cce8.jpg]

(Adj asset coupon means gross asset coupon minus the asset estimated losses which is assumed 50% of loss given default.)

Currently, Egan-Jones tends to have a more positive view of CLO credit quality compared to other credit rating agencies, as demonstrated in the table below.
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/ad5aec63-4d44-ebd9-f820-c7a1219f090c.jpg]
I. Deal Key Metrics Summary
As of March 2026, Egan-Jones rated 1670 CLO deals. We collected and calculated available deal level, tranche level and asset level key metrics such as deal weighted average rating factor and tranche subordinations, compared with prior period(s) analysis results and summarized highlights below.
I-A. Weighted Average Rating Score
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/7b545cd2-ccf9-5807-e5ac-df0c500f9a36.jpg]
Egan-Jones collected the weighted average rating score (WARS) of covered CLO deals. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the WARS value were 3607, 3697, and 3832, respectively.


(Weighted Average Rating Score is derived from 10-year default rate and used to calculate the weighted average default probability of the portfolio.)
I-B. Diversity Score
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/2b4818bc-e4fc-aa6d-e636-2650c8db9a2c.jpg]
Egan-Jones collected the Diversity Score (DS) of covered CLO deals. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the DS value were 59, 66, and 72, respectively.

(Diversity Score represents the number of independent, identical assets that we can use to mimic the default distribution of the actual portfolio.)
I-C. Super Senior Tranches Subordination
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/db679c2f-18fc-2ecd-32fb-1914b43ac68b.jpg]
Egan-Jones collected the senior tranches subordination (%) (STS) of covered CLO deals. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the STS value were 32.1, 33.5, and 35.4, respectively.

(Tranches Subordination is calculated as (Collateral Value - (Pari-Passu Balance + Senior Balance)) / Collateral Value. Defaulted assets are valued at market value.)
I-D. CCC+ or Lower Rating Percentage
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/1f390c15-1021-7c09-59a8-6bee3205b97c.jpg]
Egan-Jones collected the CCC+ and Lower Rated Asset Percentage (%) (CLRA) of covered CLO deals. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the CLRA value were 4.9, 6.5, and 9.0, respectively.
I-E. CLO Leverage Summary
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/d83229d9-8208-8ca2-0c44-a047f624d619.jpg]
Note: Deal balance is the sum of the current balance of all deal tranches; Debt balance is the sum of the current balance of all debt tranches.

Egan-Jones reviewed various liability / asset metrics. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the total deal balance to collateral balance (total current tranches balance / current collateral balance) were 93.0%, 96.0%, and 98.0%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the debt balance to collateral balance (current non-equity tranches balance / current collateral balance) were 105.0%, 106.0%, and 108.0%, respectively.
II. Tranche Key Metrics Summary
II-A. Tranche Subordination Analysis
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/cd43db59-a89f-366e-c9dc-c0316260558a.jpg]
The average subordination levels (defaulted assets are valued at market value) of senior tranches and mezzanine tranches were 36.1% and 13.4%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of senior tranche subordination levels (defaulted assets are valued at market value) were 32.3%, 33.6%, and 35.5%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of mezzanine tranche subordination levels (defaulted assets are valued at market value) were 5.7%, 10.5%, and 19.3%, respectively.
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/f64abcff-c3df-d555-4d2d-f99caa77b633.jpg]
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/f2c8c011-b0d9-8894-a3c3-b2038f1210a0.jpg]
The mean, 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the available subordination of each rating category (includes +/-) can be found in table above.
II-B. Tranche Coupon Analysis
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/cf75c8ce-ae2b-5457-f2f9-94d2dccd4e11.jpg]
The average coupon of senior tranches and mezzanine tranches is 4.9% and 7.0%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of senior tranche coupon are 4.8%, 5.0%, and 5.1%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of mezzanine tranche coupon are 5.5%, 6.4%, and 8.2%, respectively.
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/670f6887-81e1-1c44-a47d-2ad080615f34.jpg]
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/e982a92d-c1f9-7734-fb84-45c6169e9631.jpg]
The mean, 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the available coupon of each rating category (includes +/-) can be found in the table above.
II-C. Tranche Spread Analysis
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/010a225a-92dd-fc98-43b1-646b153f3841.jpg]
The average spread (over 3 months SOFR) of senior tranches and mezzanine tranches is 1.3% and 3.4%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of senior tranche spread (over 3 months SOFR) are 1.1%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of mezzanine tranche spread (over 3 months SOFR) are 1.9%, 2.8%, and 4.6%, respectively.
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/77cae8b0-8e13-f80e-4199-68153b5b5312.jpg]
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/8e6d15d0-0736-0ac7-37bb-113f8025a6a1.jpg]
The mean, 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the available spread (over 3 months SOFR) of each rating category (includes +/-) can be found in the table above.
II-D. Egan-Jones Ratings vs Other Agencies
Below is a summary of Egan-Jones ratings compared with other agencies. For the detailed full listing and sorting of Egan-Jones’s CLO ratings, please visit our website at https://portal.egan-jones.com/client/fast/clo.aspx.<https://egan-jones.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81&id=c51340a0c2&e=a1880c1820>
[https://mcusercontent.com/f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81/images/4a67ad06-cb7e-8179-321e-b5db1078cd05.jpg]
Egan-Jones's Key Rating Features & Differences Compared With Others
Below is a summary of Egan-Jones's approach (see our Methodology<https://egan-jones.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=f49cef92ca15070cd4ede9f81&id=267edf684b&e=a1880c1820> for a more complete description):

  1.  Our rating is derived from estimated losses.


  1.  The probabilities of default utilized are generally more conservative than industry standards.


  1.  Generally, our ratings are more heavily model-driven and take into account fewer subjective assumptions.


  1.  Generally, we update the cash flow and ratings monthly based on the availability of the trustee reports.


  1.  Our analysis is conducted using information and cash flow engines supplied by a recognized industry provider.


  1. Estimated Loss Information
Estimated loss is one of the key considerations in EJR's structured finance ratings. In times of stress when economic conditions are deteriorating, default rates and loss severity are more likely to increase relative to a portfolio's initial or base case default and loss severity levels. EJR believes a tranche with higher rating should be able to withstand greater stress and sustain lower losses than a tranche with a lower rating. For example, a tranche with AAA rating should be able to survive the great depression scenario (the highest default and loss severity levels experienced if they were to occur in the future). A 'AA' rated tranche would be more susceptible to an adverse economic impact than the 'AAA' rated tranche but nonetheless should be able to withstand such effects better than a tranche with a lower rating. Nach der zuletzt beispiellosen verbalen Eskalation aus dem Munde des US-Präsidenten fällt die Erleichterung über die überraschend vereinbarte Waffenruhe zwischen den Kriegsparteien am Golf umso größer aus, auch an den Finanzmärkten. Wir haben die heutige Entwicklung in verschiedenen Stücken für Sie aufbereitet:

  *   Nicht nur die Aktienindizes stiegen nach Bekanntwerden der Waffenruhe kräftig. Auch bei anderen Anlagen wie Gold, Silber, Bitcoin sowie am Renten- und Ölmarkt ist die Entspannung spürbar. Allerdings bleiben Zweifel angesichts der Unberechenbarkeit von Donald Trump (79), der gestern noch wüst mit der Auslöschung von Irans Zivilisation gedroht hatte. Es müsse sich erst zeigen, ob die Feuerpause auch halte, so der Tenor unter Analysten. Meine Kollegen Kai Lange und Lutz Reiche geben einen Überblick über die Marktreaktionen und die Faktoren, auf die es jetzt ankommt<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D>.

Die für den Welthandel so wichtige Meerenge wird damit zum Testfall: Werden Schiffe tatsächlich wieder ungehindert passieren können? Derzeit sitzen mehr als 2000 Handelsschiffe im Persischen Golf fest, Berichten zufolge wollen die Iraner in nächster Zeit eine Durchfahrtsgebühr von 2 Millionen Dollar pro Schiff <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D> kassieren. Nicht nur deshalb zeigen sich Reedereien vorerst zurückhaltend und wollen die Lage erst mal prüfen, bevor sie ihre Schiffe am Golf in Gang setzen.

  *   Wie der Ölpreis sinkt heute auch der Preis für Erdgas. Entscheidend für die weitere Entwicklung beim Gas<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?%3D%3D> sei aber weniger die Wasserstraße von Hormus als vielmehr die Wiederinbetriebnahme des im Krieg beschädigten weltgrößten LNG-Hubs Ras Laffan in Katar, sagen Marktbeobachter.

Brauns Verteidigungsstrategie droht zu scheitern  und eine Verurteilung rückt womöglich näher. AI agents in retail investing

People do not like to lose money on stocks. Sometimes a stock goes down, and people who own it sell it to avoid losing more money, so it goes down more. This behavior is to some extent predictable, so there are circumstances in which you might think<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Bg376sF7KW8UbFNHyimAWoDl_TThQj_vtykDNNz7WLE27Lvvmpn6lfGMkZxo5oRGOcZHyQRXXg3UfKzyT0mGJeYjSSIi7mIx7opIarRHroMAhtfn_-DCKIsROc6YZEnaOpwC-YLnZQEQlTE9X0VpLZblfI2nQVC_jLzY6uvKJJIQgQdlMR6aYHP0mzewO3fQMJ1BQZJJ5Vfd3moEAJJBZinEwvirzikm0BrLBVLl4rInRFCO7EiE9ieCH8meIiD9UIGTgbfuefNE9wNlwOC-yys6Ku1PM_xgDQN4FFmt7tzK2ArLtEMXUbgAppV6Fl7E5vM0Nd49pxNl4_MIcLnUd3BsViWEBC1MbXtJRZGHGPJGUorYJBb8QRb0nw/yVZV_n9eNtu-wOJIGQbhHl9bvlxREMX0/19> if this stock goes below $50, it will probably keep going down to $45. You might think that as a pure matter of investor psychology: If the stock goes below $50, a lot of people who bought it at $50 will have losses and panic and hit the sell button, driving it down more.

You might have a slightly different theory. Because people do not like to lose money on stocks, and are not monitoring their stocks constantly, they might use stop-loss orders<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/C1N9UoeNt3Dbz8ysDHEWuZ79OcQKFGxoEZAbBPgtjtcO43_18Xtyj1Sb-oMtzImsz8RkLwF_gl4hPmqq8BctnWe8D_66cbaFuRGrIYq7FrLjFRCGrdMONBX8vnsAQMkch2amPU9sFyrXmqjly6avxU5KqTozEl2CA04bwetLm1923LQhFMfC8SY5NOCXI9hmAo4e82HBy_g0sNQQDR9r_WkfOgzZJdFIBq7Ct43Y2es08XrGjgoHYeQv81h2Al214npwPHKVLHFyib5wrokeK_8wx4I2_HoPUsw7vss8fP-cDO26wu4OFuF4i2Y6YZcqPLReOG3S2A66Hy71KSLxCmn7VGgmqo9lDZUxoZ3Q3vxIC86LbJ591d1CEw/C3YlrfZMgsFv9GJYN5C82R-sabFGIxiM/19>, where they tell their broker if this stock goes below $50, sell it immediately. Intuitively, people who do this are more likely to use round numbers like $50 than, like, if this stock goes below $51.37, sell it, so there is some clustering of stop-loss orders; there are more of them at some numbers than at others. And so if you are trying to predict market behavior, you might think if this stock goes below $50, a lot of people will automatically sell it, and it will go down to $45. None of this is investing or technical-analysis advice, but a certain<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/zYTSBMFCnYzq6s8sddspDT7WYHSwPD3jk0Lt4Rzg4MC4zKuJhPag8hlsC5xmeNWb3NI_9_2j8n_bh9fuylWEOHYj8SP0xCoApweyw1L2SO0OmLZOiXRisn002sO1aybLt4qGIaYZa18ZQhzjHBHB3s19Ys0Nm_dOkGAVl4RWFGO7GQ_8lbL5OjAljdoe_Ti2MYGAww4jXURKp78t27m1IaCLhOce4pynbJmCkX8MvJ5AOauA9ozwNTpEMi3qv0TIxHbq6YVcK-0oG4P7HnlEs-GXMmECN4KkM0l4sWDuCTnKBdSTIYmBuf2lylPDcRXAOJ8F5Vh4mgXbYNgTQNFL2HNICASP6OI0w8rXnKyaaAFRMOmPj0hGPpdzJw/T0dMsliHs9qFJUsMgaxUc6TC0w3wFiG9/19> amount<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-wiEmly2EPAAZ4z-fnz4MlWwpsyg83pFmeShmTMRGHhbjgQBZEyGwMP1jELvi8YPIurChBTpx4sigrvt3WV_Sz4L3sIZmlPByid8mO9I8pWXmCaDHDEefUvJLGucZfOjg6GCgc9vDsffwbHaxCvXthIvsrKsd9hIGeKcP_15L3U4fpzlOteQeHBklkFEhtO0MTJY8Im9DtsMcIn3wibdVCSlCfSMnOqmPt8g-qAANCjn95xLTKtTTKqvS8WtFpJcDUXlOJg5JbjTF_LJgkWV2GynJ6N7ZxENTPxKue9jj8pBcmS-Tkno0hlRUUfwAjBsci_lkc3N3k_Q9sFYCxBgWhGTjStrLMagcO7x8Feq2G7Zms8lZY3LQRZ8tw/xAcMENpGQw3_YrUOBrSdwM3zdv3vuCXX/19> of stop hunting probably goes on in financial markets: If you know or suspect that a lot of people have stop-loss orders to sell if a stock falls to $50, you might try to short the stock until it hits $50, expecting to trigger the stops and buy it back at $45.

In a sense, the previous two paragraphs express the same idea: They both say people have irrational biases that make them anchor on round numbers and fear losses, so if the stock falls to $50 there will be further irrational selling driving it down to $45. The difference is the mechanism: In the first paragraph, the stock hits $50 and then people decide to sell; in the second paragraph, people plan ahead to sell if the stock hits $50, and automate that selling. But the second paragraph feels more real, more predictable: I know there are stop orders to sell at $50, so if the stock falls below $50 it will keep going down has a bit more science to it than I think people will panic at $50 and sell more.

This point might generalize. Like:

  1.  Everything that happens in financial markets reflects, in some way, investor psychology. If you have a good aggregate sense of how investors think about stuff, and stuff happens, then you can predict whether asset prices will go up or down. But this is very hard and somewhat fuzzy, and if you said I have perfect insight into how investors think so give me money to start a hedge fund, people might not believe you. (If you have empirical insight into some narrower behavioral point  Indian retail investors buy way more options than underlying shares, say<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/KvHbO1x2APtbwRBGlQzHDkMv-Gc469RTAg0v5roKqw9K0o05RW7KNfYS1iDzSaFg62dmTKlKmYSWBDYngWvmPaiYHaHjk2DN351RZwzjD6r0HeB1rBDGveWqIAP7h-oheXFmC2g858LHVQSnrgX1fZ7XJ3QNHRfK-2LPjv4zpI12wsptQDdm1KXLvY0eNCTcHPTdg9seIhVFfyz89c_ucxvIgb0Rk5fdeG1tVVzNKiO_I-zvoFs6Sr-sAArb5wT4o3DKOG3pNdSGwfddcW0dcS2Cp6Fxs_WDrZ7CXWYOTA36zT6HdZ3Ec8pAY9jbRc5JKnWKKSaJjxxAQXJ-abFBZgusgGnPDHjctTDlLQyOATbiFZP38f1pGBkkUw/JyB9LjjLypzqSlN5GjwuKbiz-_zmRURF/19>  then that might be a useful strategy.)
  2.  Some things that happen in financial markets  some small but notable subset of the things in the previous paragraph reflect automated or rule-based investor psychology. Investors think if X happens I should do Y, and they set up an automated process to do Y if X happens, and if you have a good aggregate sense of what processes they have automated and how, you can predict whether asset prices will go up or down. This is not easy, necessarily, but it feels like more of an exact science than simply predicting investor psychology, and you probably can do it at a hedge fund. When new stocks are added to the index, index funds mechanically sell the old stocks and buy the new ones: That is a quasi-automation of investor desires, and predicting it is definitely a hedge fund strategy<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/izgixcWWMLlxW7d7KAi56s0sbsSSD2xn73Yg7QQ-QurzqGLXLLMI_cUyffpqwiCqliDLJQn6GEMdRnCFc312Zq-MRcbsYAnDMqBdxsXUgcE2m_Xxu4DVTPRaR9cpvZUE9q8NAwW-J1Llu0E7SxYYOArbiZPSiZodEqES3uHo3xq8gQkhp7Q6mHATpyIrXocRTcShIK88yErBQ-3gytA4bqSW19Yam09eTM9Cdgz0pe7Uo5V3JfvgWiFMc3WYxKn0tN2iumculflbruqTsn6vYbMjLfcVNMnnC_FRz-unBQJpkFfnqFtbs0WJw0IAIW3S3DxETmRfVUjSlHJNyyKDpsdUrX1ZYvV-suDzuwYsCtlpBKjG2Nk1bAY4aCQ/qvbx0jAoy5-Nf01A7FIGFPBcBj1dU_gv/19>. When a bond goes from a BBB- rating to BB+, investment-grade bond funds have to sell it, and its price falls more than is justified by fundamentals<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/EYCRcYZVzyqN6kDEkCTPRfIfv9e53gDq2cYeiC12VwcZWc9XlkyPpNCp6MsaVh3z6OBCxVMvlLLtfYlNJf_YbyHwaQ4uGEmIMIvZuP_bi4GJfDwDKLM8-I3buv9jTZm42LUsKhKcB3TB_SUXChO1-n5R_CjE_y57oTmJrtRBmYXFlh2g4JTladwt3v6f8h0p3m0YKj6ugRIPlct9TlTxDBPPJ2JZsLqJ1WvQAtntsRRhfLOPbXvYT_nmxI7q6SEwxSTK03IFQLRDibFbO2LKWNfVvSsVIGJ1F62SusvUGGdur6g70oEvFhKEnHGviERZh6GnHg8PK7YHC87Q9FdyfGXh9jDt6cvLxTc8AmXCtulOo7lc-BQRwqEfrx0/R4bInpvK9FXyORes6sodA9th9G9W_fCh/19>: That again is a story about investor psychology (people like to own safe bonds) that has been turned into a mechanical rule (investment-grade funds have to own bonds with investment-grade ratings).

The examples in the previous paragraph  index rebalancing, fallen-angel bonds  are about institutional investors, because institutional investors are, you know, institutions. They have rules and procedures and mandates and regulation; they behave predictably. Retail investors just do what they want. They sometimes act predictably, but they tend not to automate their predictable behavior, aside from the occasional stop-loss order. [1] You might think retail investors tend to buy the dip, so if the stock market is down more than 2% near the close today, I should buy some stock to profit from tomorrows retail dip-buying, and you might be right. But the retail buyers might all change their minds or forget; their dip-buying is just a descriptive matter of psychology. Its not like they have all set up automated rules-based systems to buy the dip.

The dispersion trade, which buys options on individual US stocks while selling those on the broader index, suffered a 4.9% loss last month, the steepest since 2011 in backtested data, an index from JPMorgan Chase & Co. shows. Bank swaps tied to the approach fell 2.6%, according to Premialab, which aggregates industry data.

The losses lay bare the strategys vulnerability to such a major geopolitical event. As the conflict in Iran escalated, investors rushed to hedge at the index level, driving implied volatility on the S&P 500 sharply higher. At the same time, individual stocks began moving in lockstep  collapsing precisely the divergence between single-name and benchmark volatility that the dispersion trade is designed to harvest.

The recent events had macro consequences on oil, commodities, inflation, rates, rather than micro impacts at the single-stock level, Luca Valitutti, managing director for exotics and hybrids trading at Citigroup Inc., wrote in an email. Correlation between single stocks has spiked.

We talked about this<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/sJXFKXjWQwMmb5xdzNVYdm8RHjMXMnpMM9zqgbKMct8MFGKjZ2a6aDPeXUZfTjtTt410F8NnS9fvha5KBN8weGUDp4FhQ6EBWfCLGv1zigq0cjj8WEYOhSvoisB4qpefh9zH6sc17N5ld-62J7iLXYbHyjyCdJqN8JSc2ZwcpWdVe63IeO-iQQX8HkM7Dlaj2zvmI_hFbZtmGhwIVMot-7l0RV1QxeNu2CuWjRUzu8lLBtV6TaVq0Oj43HSDyMjKcU52hwPWdAzLJJGGk-Ov43PwLbENnc0fOzGAv2nBFOO_G7CyHI7sdOzgeNO43GBMhTvdBEW9HEywHliAvCx4XCXGFmrhN2fxsRsCgprYcU0Cce24Bbvg7719FIU/GdXvXJsc9rgA7DJ9t6tfoGtxTkLiw18r/19> at the beginning of last month. The dispersion trade is, classically, a bet on stereotypical behavior by investors: They like to buy index options to hedge broad market risk, and they like to sell single-stock options for income. Therefore index options trade at a premium and single-stock options trade at a discount, and you can manufacture index options out of single-stock options to capture that spread. [3]

But it is also a fundamental bet on correlation. If individual stocks are volatile but uncorrelated, then their volatility will cancel each other out: Some stocks will go up 2%, some will go down 1.5%, and the overall stock index will go up 0.5%. Index volatility will be lower than single-stock volatility, and a strategy of buying single-stock options and selling index options will make a lot of money. [4] If individual stocks all move together, then theyll all go up 2% today and down 1.5% tomorrow, the overall index will go up 2% today and down 1.5% tomorrow, index volatility will be high and youll lose money on the dispersion trade. [5]

As we discussed last month, a reasonable fundamental story in February was something like the rise of artificial intelligence is going to create huge winners and huge losers, so there will be a lot of dispersion among stocks. And February was a great month for the dispersion trade. Auditing

There are various sophisticated forms of accounting fraud, where you can exploit nuances of accounting rules and blind spots of auditors to inflate your companys assets or revenues. But there is also the simplest form of accounting fraud, where you have 1,000 widgets in inventory and just write down that you have 10,000. That is not especially difficult for your auditors to spot: They can just go to your widget warehouse and count the widgets. But thats easy for me to say, here, typing on my computer. If you are the auditor sent out to the widget warehouse, just count 10,000 widgets might not sound that easy.. Here is a Wall Street Journal story about auditors praying for AI to replace them<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/27BlkNc41pMc0KER_8rwJK0CCHnaQx1mmRlgTP1QpFG6m71GgHagJBVmjmjlDYD4BxeY2vW-78rf9EhTA3KshfkjFo6tzVjmk7sY5w2_Int18w8sZkJ5TO9rgiKKh71ZZIAZ6EdC2_tbKeB7EttJoJc9RoFxHAim4R1sVv_4aEwnhnk4Age7Qhnvtg7nFHsOQMG8i0nu4pYJ9-dTLGVRg-1z2-GPgjJ1BHybcn0nOm3Te0uHJVeHL-zWHkc-lQEDEipxUABrhgWCWJCp12YXjBrVAn1_oDQjnnqvn3-LJR1jpEyg2Cw1n9nVXir94Eu1AQaJlFGfI62lI7sAm7GfExMhZ8dHfkqbwG2JzGFVxWWgtL1qUyfSxpBhV6k/YDWKU8hR2yO81h-Y-GsGm8Wb0ysZj1Jj/19>:

Accounting firms and their clients are increasingly using artificial intelligence and drones to do work long handled by humans. But so far, theres been no technological solution to what is often the dirtiest part of an audit: counting inventory. That means the messy, bizarre field trips remain a rite of passage for young professionals in an otherwise deskbound field. ...

Auditors are often tasked with traveling to the middle of nowhere and tallying up a large amount of unusual things, from chickens and pigs to quarry rocks, corn, traffic lights and telephone poles. They complain about ending up covered in manure or dust, or shivering in a freezer.

The large accounting firms typically rely on junior auditors to do much of the dirty work. The trips provide an opportunity to learn more about clients. But in the moment, they stink. Gen Z auditors share horror stories on social media. I just counted thousands and thousands of nuts and bolts. What did you do today?? one posted on TikTok. A Reddit user said they were sent to count rocks in below-freezing weather, including a pile in a snake-infested quarry.

We used to talk all the time about the idea that the blockchain would prevent fraud, guarantee the provenance of goods, etc., and I was always skeptical: Really good computer technology can prevent all sorts of computer-based fraud and manipulation, but there is always going to be some nexus between the computers and the physical world, and you cant count on the computer to monitor that nexus. Eventually I suppose AI will get good enough to police that nexus  humanoid robots with sophisticated eyes will walk into the warehouse and instantly say I count 162,385 nuts and 237,423 bolts, whats next?  but for now it is, uh, maybe the last job for humans.
